author: groundxero
title: After 9/11, the ‘War on Terror’ Was a War of Terror
content:
The crusade that George W. Bush launched 25 years ago to “rid the world of evil” only compounded it.


 


Norman Solomon


Sep 09, 2026


 


Three days after terrorists killed almost 3,000 people in the 

United States

 on September 11, 2001, President 

George W. Bush

 stood behind a pulpit at the 

Washington

 National Cathedral and spoke to a nation in shock. “Our responsibility to history is already clear,” he 

proclaimed

, “to answer these attacks and rid the world of evil.” The vow was, of course, preposterous. Yet the “war on terror” that followed was scarcely more realistic.


 


“Terrorism is not an enemy. It cannot be defeated. It’s a tactic,” retired US Army General William Odom 

told

 C-SPAN viewers in 2002. “It’s about as sensible to say we declare war on night attacks and expect we’re going to win that war. We’re not going to win the war on terrorism.” But the American military crusade became more about persisting than winning. The ultraviolent momentum became its own reason. The destructive search for enemies created more. As years went by and the “war on terror” label faded, US warfare was so normal in so many places that it no longer needed a name or much of a rationale.


 


But 25 years ago, the impulse to avenge the horrors of 

9/11

 

was instant. Fear and rage blended into high octane for war machinery. Suddenly, overwhelming public emotions were fully in sync with the psychology of a 

military-industrial complex

 set for large-scale killing.


 


Even as the trauma of the terrible day eased for the general public, 9/11 continued to serve as a political license to kill without an expiration date.


 


None of the 

19 hijackers

 were Afghan, and Al Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden’s ties were much tighter with 

Saudi Arabia

, but his presence in Afghanistan put that country in the Pentagon’s gunsights. The question in US media was not about whether, but when, to attack. The answer came on October 7 when American missiles began to explode in Afghanistan. Hours later, a Gallup 

poll

 found that “90 percent of Americans approve of the United States taking such military action, while just 5 percent are opposed, and another 5 percent are unsure.”


 


The air war remained quite popular in the United States. Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld held daily live televised briefings that catapulted him to national adulation. A pattern set in, taking for granted that American warfare was beneficent in intent and benign in meaningful impact. People dying 

under American bombs

 and 

less directly


didn’t count for much. “The targeting capabilities, and the care that goes into targeting, to see that the precise targets are struck, and that other targets are not struck, is as impressive as anything anyone could see, Rumsfeld 

asserted

. And he added, “The weapons that are being used today have a degree of precision that no one ever dreamt of.”


 


Rumsfeld’s style went over big. “Everyone is genuflecting before the 

Pentagon

 powerhouse,” 

exclaimed

 the Washington Post’s media reporter, Howard Kurtz, who called Rumsfeld “America’s new rock star.” That winter, after the 

Taliban

 government fell, the host of NBC’s Meet the Press program 

congratulated

 Rumsfeld on the air: “Sixty-nine years old and you’re America’s stud.”


 


The war in Iraq, launched with a March 2003 invasion, relied on massive air power and more than 150,000 US ground troops. The 

Saddam Hussein

 dictatorship fell quickly, but the 

promised “cakewalk”

 turned into year after year of combat and slaughter. Mainstream US media outlets were more than comfortable with above-it-all bombing that signified American air prowess. But the toll of American deaths and severe injuries gradually depleted enthusiasm as soldiers were called back for two, three or even more tours of duty. For many, the images of glory days turned into real-life nightmares.


 


The ongoing war effort that began in autumn 2001 had an implicit throughline in dominant media and politics: while American lives really matter, the victims of American firepower really don’t.


 


President Bush could not accept defeat in Iraq, and later 

Barack Obama

 could not countenance defeat in Afghanistan. Early in his presidency, Obama—in deed and word—made the “war on terror” expressly bipartisan. Less than a year after he received the 

Nobel Peace Prize

 in late 2009, the American troop level in Afghanistan reached 100,000, triple the number …

author: rti_admin
title: India’s Gen-Z Movement: Challenges Ahead for the Teachers and the Buddhist Way Forward
content:
The resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan, Minister of Education, Government of India (a Gen-X person born between 1965–1980), has come as a shock, as it was considered impossible to get a resignation from any minister of the Narendra Modi-led NDA government from 2014 till now. However, the students of Gen-Z (born between 1997–2012, now in the age group 14–29) made it possible, along with the Millennials (born between 1981–1996), Gen-X, and Gen-Alpha (born between 2013–2020). The Gen-Z students would be mostly from class 10th onwards, and some may be working professionals as well. The protests (mostly) by Gen-Z have shown the other generations that they have accomplished something that other generations could not have achieved in the last 12 years (although the support of other generations cannot be neglected). The Gen-Z students would then have a new level of confidence when they go to their classes and interact with their teachers. However, without the right guidance to channel it properly, this surge of confidence can easily tip into an obdurate, impudent, and supercilious attitude, turning their outlook entirely quixotic. Therefore, the role of teachers, supervisors, universities, institutes, etc., would come into the picture, and they would have to face certain challenges. The challenges mentioned are not exhaustive; instead, they are suggestive.

The first challenge that universities/institutes (overall) and individual teachers as well would face is: Are the Gen-Z students going to listen (śravaṇa in Sanskrit—the first step of learning) to their teachers and universities? Are they going to follow the rules and regulations of the university/institute and maintain the decorum of the classes? Why I think this may be a challenge is because the Gen-Z students, with their creativity of language and presentation, have shut the mouths of many mainstream media channels and politicians, and have also astonished political scientists who never expected the occurrence of this nation-wide protest (if not in India, then at least not under the present government). These students have not been in the mood to listen to anything that has no bearing on the government’s accountability for the suicides of many NEET aspirants. This is understandable considering the seriousness of the issue. However, some videos have shown that students have hooted at the biased media channels, as they have been determined not to listen to anything from them.

The second challenge deals with humility and humbleness. Humility is an important aspect of learning. Learning results in humility (as said, vidyā dadāti vinayaṁ). Learning also results from humility—if I think that I am superior to others in terms of knowledge, how can I learn from others? I would then do whatever I think is fit according to ‘me’, even if that act disrespects someone. Are the Gen-Z students going to contemplate their continuous learning from life (manan in Sanskrit—the second step for learning), or would they feel supercilious? Are the Gen-Z students going to be in the disposition to learn from their teachers? Why I think this may be a challenge is because the Gen-Z students have already contemplated the inevitable consequences of the ruining of the country if the lacuna in education is not fixed. For this, they have raised their voice for their right to education, and thereby they have taught the world the peaceful management of crowds, connecting people, and leading a crowd. However, this same sense of achievement may let them feel that they know everything. It is also possible that they may not contemplate new learning, reflect deeply, or sharpen their arguments and creativity. Rather, they may take refuge in harsh and abusive language to assert their points, which has already been seen in the protests by some of the students. This aggression might block any novel and meaningful discoveries in their learning journey.

The third challenge is the continuity and culmination of the above two and deals with real-life experiences (nidhidhyāsana). The real-life experiences of unexpected events occur only when we listen to others and continuously contemplate them. Without that, we would continuously live in one set of habituated thinking caused by our external environments. But by continuously listening to others, like our well-wishers—teachers, parents, friends, etc.—and critics, we would be able to contemplate and improve our habituated practices. But without checks and balances …

author: Editors
title: 9/11: How the US turned tragedy into barbarity
content:
Twenty-five years ago, the world changed irrevocably. Not because terrorists from the al-Qaeda network attacked the United States, bringing down the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers in New York, hitting the Pentagon in Virginia and killing nearly 3,000 people. It changed because of US imperialism’s response.

The day after 9/11, the editors of

Socialist Alternative

 magazine, one of the precursor publications of

Red Flag

, warned: “The real threat to people around the world is not terrorism, but the racism, militarism, repression and nationalism that has been unleashed in the wake of the terrorist attacks”.

A week later, President George W. Bush, in an address to a joint session of Congress, announced his so-called War on Terror: “Every nation, in every region, now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists”. His administration rode the wave of outrage over al-Qaeda’s assault to open a new era of imperialist aggression that has cost millions of people’s lives. 

First came Afghanistan in October. It didn’t matter that the ruling Taliban

offered to hand over Osama bin Laden

, the alleged mastermind of the terrorist attacks, to a neutral country to face trial. The US was interested only in war. Condoleezza Rice, then Bush’s national security adviser, admitted as much to the

New Yorker

’s Nicholas Lemann several months later. In the wake of the 9/11 attacks, she had asked senior national security staff to think about how to “capitalise on these opportunities”. 

The Bush administration soon began making a public case for invading Iraq—which had no ties to 9/11—declaring the country part of an “axis of evil” with Iran and North Korea. Undersecretary of State John Bolton soon expanded the axis list to include Cuba, Libya and Syria. The bombs started raining down on Baghdad in March 2003.

These invasions would have been followed by more had the resistance in Iraq not bogged down the US military in an intractable counterinsurgency. Nevertheless, Brown University’s

Costs of War research

 estimates the direct death toll from US military operations in the post-9-11 era in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan to be close to 1 million people. It estimates a further 3.6 to 3.8 million “indirect” deaths resulting from the “destruction of economies, healthcare systems, infrastructure and the environment”. 

The US also set up a global kidnapping network, which it termed “extraordinary rendition”, and a series of “black sites” in which prisoners were held without charge and tortured.

The Open Society Foundation estimates

 that 54 governments collaborated in the program. Then there is the notorious

Guantánamo Bay torture camp

, used since 2002 and still holding ageing prisoners from the War on Terror. This all served as notice that the US empire would stop at nothing to maintain its global domination.

A more enduring legacy of this era of “forever wars” has been the construction of vast internal security and surveillance states, which have trampled civil and democratic rights. 

More than 140 governments have adopted “counterterrorism” legislation since 9/11, beginning with the USA PATRIOT Act, which green-lit mass surveillance and delayed-notice search warrants and bolstered spy agency resources. Mega-departments, such as Homeland Security in the US and Home Affairs in Australia, were established as Western states have become more authoritarian.

Indeed, Australia is one of the worst offenders. “No other nation can match the volume of Australia’s counter-terrorism laws”, wrote legal academics Rebecca Ananian-Welsh and Keiran Hardy in

a 2021 piece for the University of Queensland’s

Contact

 magazine

. They describe the scope of the laws as “staggering”, “unprecedented” and “extreme”, noting that they go beyond even “historical wartime powers”.

They include control orders, preventive detention, and compulsory retention of all telecommunication and online data of every resident. The

Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Act

 of 2021 gave law enforcement agencies the power to take control of a person’s individual online accounts, modify or delete their data and even take over entire networks. That is, they can legally alter a person’s text messages.

Death and destruction abroad and authoritarianism at home: such is the “rules-based order”, the purported demise of which we are supposed to lament. This post-9/11 era normalised authoritarianism …

author: Susan Price
title: Singapore’s unfinished anti-colonial struggle
content:
The dominant history of modern Singapore was meticulously constructed under the banner of the “Singapore Story”. By presenting the material interests of the ruling elite as the universal interests of the nation, the state narrative reduces the mass anti-imperialist movement of the mid-20th century into a fable; one wherein a heroic bourgeois leadership single-handedly navigates a vulnerable island state through the perils of communism to construct a prosperous capitalist metropolis.

In his six-part oral history series with Pintjin (PJ) Thum, Dr Poh Soo Kai, former student activist, co-founder of the People’s Action Party (PAP) and the Barisan Sosialis (Socialist Front) — and former political prisoner detained for nearly 17 years without trial — delivers a vital historical materialist counter-narrative.

In 36 minutes of personal testimony, Poh unpacks the class dynamics, state coercion, and geopolitical shake-ups that dismantled working-class power and shaped Singapore's transition into a disciplined capitalist state.

Poh begins by recalling how post-World War II Malayan households were adorned with portraits of Indonesia’s Sukarno, India’s Nehru and Gandhi, and China’s Chiang Kai-Shek, who were seen as regional anti-colonial leaders. The struggle in Singapore was bound to broader anti-imperialist movements across Malaya, Indonesia, and Vietnam.

Poh’s account of the 1954 Fajar Trial undermines the state’s origin myth, which positions the trial of eight members of the editorial board of Fajar (Dawn) — the University of Malaya Socialist Club’s newspaper — as Lee Kuan Yew’s (LKY’s) personal legal breakthrough.

[Editor’s note: Harry Lee Kwan Yew co-founded the PAP, was a barrister and opposition figure and became Singapore’s first Prime Minister in 1959.]

As president of the University of Malaya Socialist Club, Poh helped publish Fajar, an anti-colonial paper opposing the anti-communist South East Asian Treaty Organisation (SEATO) and foreign military bases. When the editorial board was charged with sedition, Queen’s Counsel DN Pritt arrived to lead the defense. Poh recounts Pritt greeting him warmly at the Dolphin Hotel before turning to LKY, who was acting as local junior counsel, and saying, “Harry, now you can go.”

Pritt dismissed LKY specifically to formulate an anti-colonial strategy directly with the student activists, recognising that the trial was a political battlefield rather than a legal technicality.

This moment symbolises the clash between the radical student movement and LKY’s legalism, and how official history later repackaged a left-wing victory as an LKY solo masterstroke.

As the PAP rose to power, internal contradictions between its left-wing mass base and moderate leadership erupted.

Poh recounts how the left wing consistently pushed for true self-determination, confronting PAP Chair Toh Chin Chye to issue a public statement supporting then-Chief Minister David Marshall’s 1956 call for internal self-rule — a move that infuriated LKY upon his return from London.

[Editor’s note: Marshall was appointed Chief Minister after contesting the 1955 election as a candidate for the Labour Front. After failing to secure self-rule, he resigned as Chief Minister in June 1956.]

Chief Minister Lim Yew Hock’s violent crackdowns on trade unions and Chinese school students from 1956 onward served a dual purpose: suppressing working-class organisation while allowing LKY to position himself as the sensible alternative acceptable to British imperial interests and local capital.

When dissident MPs and activists walked out to form the Barisan Sosialis in 1961, every PAP branch including LKY’s own Tanjong Pagar constituency defected to the new party. The PAP was left as a hollow electoral vessel without organic mass support.

To preempt an electoral defeat, the state deployed Operation Coldstore in February 1963. Officially framed as a security operation against a communist plot tied to the 1962 Brunei Revolt, Coldstore was a draconian political purge that sought to decapitate the political opposition, dismantle union leadership and ensure PAP hegemony.

The state weaponised identity politics to divide the multi-ethnic working-class by branding Chinese-educated labour leaders and Barisan Sosialis members as “Chinese chauvinists”. It replaced class-based solidarity with state-directed multiracialism that contained labour organising within non-threatening boundaries.

Declassified British colonial intelligence …

author: AWSM
title: The anarchist case for abstentionism in elections
content:
The right to vote is seen by most as a necessary prerequisite for freedom across the world. People have fought and died for the right to vote in elections. Women across the world fought bitter battles for the right to vote. So why should anarchists question this as a right worth having?

The entire electoral show is designed to encourage us to believe that not only does our vote matter, but that it is the most important decision we could possibly make. Indeed, voting is held so sacred by many that the mere mention of not voting is enough to cause outrage. Pointing out that our vote makes no difference anyway, will see you accused of being apathetic, privileged, immature, and even being part of the alt-right!

But as noted anarchist Vernon Richards wrote,

“So long as we have capitalism and government, the job of anarchists is to fight both, and at the same time encourage people to take what steps they can to run their own lives.” [“Anarchists and Voting,” pp. 176–87, The Raven, No. 14, p. 179].

Electoralism ensures that a statist perspective becomes dominant. Everything is seen in terms of state intervention and following the decisions of the leaders, which has always proved deadly to encouraging a spirit of revolt, self-management, and self-help – the very keys to creating change in a society. Rather than being something other people discuss on behalf of working-class people, anarchists argue that politics should not be a specialised activity in the hands of the so-called experts (i.e., politicians) but instead lie in the hands of those directly affected by it in the process of participation, direct action, and self-management. Those that channel any “political” conclusions into electoral politics distort discussions into only what is possible within the current system. Given this, is it surprising that anarchists argue that the people “must organise their powers apart from and against the State?” [Bakunin, The Political Philosophy of Bakunin, p. 376].

Abstentionists get told, “If you don’t vote, you have no right to complain about the outcome,” but we consider the opposite to be true. It is those who have voted, who have agreed to the rules, and agreed to be governed by the winners who cannot complain. It is those who do not participate who have the right to complain about the outcome more than anyone else.

We get told that the reality is that voting does change things, but we can, and do, deny that. Voting attempts to provide the population with the illusion of change while in reality it reinforces the current system. A policy here and there may change, the faces may change, but the system of a wealthy minority ruling a poorer majority remains. People will continually be telling us that abstaining from voting will help the right-wing win the election, that it is better if the lesser evil wins. This may possibly be the case (although the argument is far from convincing), but why should we base our society on a compromise with evil? In fact, the “progressive” left wing party you vote for will often be ready to take the same actions as a right-wing government when it comes to imposing anti-working-class action upon us, (as we shall show later in this essay the state has a corrupting effect on those who enter politics with high principles). There should be a better way, and we say the dismantling of government, in all its existing and potential forms is that way.

Most of the left wing in Aotearoa, and quite a few people who claim to identify as anarchists, will support reformist parties in the upcoming election. You will hear them saying things like “vote Labour (or Green) without illusions,” or “vote Labour/Green but build a socialist alternative.” The slogans that these others may shout only reflect the idea that change can and should be brought about by a small number of elite politicians. Abstentionists do not say things like this. There are many problems with our electoral system of democracy, which we shall run through, but we must state that first and foremost, as anarchists, we see voting as against running contrary to our anti-statist and anti-hierarchy principles, and we see electoralism as contrary to our goals and practice. It reinforces the idea that society is divided into order-givers and order-takers. Famed French anarchist, Elisee Reclus, put it well when he said,

“Everything that can be said about the suffrage may be summed up in a sentence. To vote is to give up your own power. To elect a …

author: Editors
title: FROM THE ARCHIVE—Tragedy in America: how should the left respond? (12 September 2001)
content:
Today, there is no shortage of mainstream commentators prepared to speak out strongly against the war policy of the George W. Bush era. Even current US President Donald Trump claims to have been an opponent of the Iraq invasion and of the broader orientation of the Republican administration of 2001-09.

But in the days after 9/11, no major media outlet would hear a word against the US. Those of us who said that US imperialism, not terrorism, posed the greatest threat to the world were vilified, marginalised and condemned as terrorist sympathisers.

Socialist Alternative is proud that we took an unequivocal anti-imperialist stance, even in those early and dark days when doing so was deeply unpopular. The article republished below was put out on 12 September 2001. We think its arguments, unlike so much written then and since, stand the test of time.

Socialist Alternative

 magazine editorial

The September 11 attacks in New York and Washington, D.C., are a horrific tragedy.

The bodies of thousands of ordinary working-class people—of all races, religions and political beliefs—lie in the rubble of New York’s World Trade Centre.

But the response of the world’s leaders, and of the media commentators and opinion writers, has been marked by a hideous hypocrisy.

US President George Bush, along with others such as Tony Blair, and our own John Howard and Kim Beazley, have fallen over themselves to condemn terrorism, violence and murder.

They have vowed to fight the “uncivilised” actions of people who they accuse of having no regard for the sanctity of human life. But it is the likes of Bush, Blair and Howard who preside over a system that condemns millions to death and misery all around the world.

Up to 200,000 civilians were murdered in the oil-driven Gulf War in 1991. More than 500,000 children have died since as a result of crippling sanctions.

Around the world—in Indonesia, the Middle East, Africa and Latin America—despotic regimes financed and supported by the US government have slaughtered hundreds of thousands of people.

The genocide of one-third of the East Timorese population was directly supported by the US, Australia and Britain. The brutal Israeli occupation of Palestine is propped up by the $1.5 billion in aid it receives from the US every year.

And the logic of the capitalist system has condemned millions to death through war and poverty around the globe. 20,000 children starve to death and die of preventable diseases every day because US grain is dumped in the ocean to keep prices up, and because multinationals conspire to stop medical treatments being accessible to the world’s poor.

And while George Bush rails against terrorism, the fact is that Bin Laden, accused of being behind the September 11 attacks, shares with Timothy McVeigh the distinction of having been trained in terrorism by the US government.

The CIA trained Bin Laden as a commander in its proxy army that fought the USSR after its invasion of Afghanistan in 1979. Bin Laden was “so effective a recruiter [for the Afghan guerrillas] that close comrades at the time actually thought he was working for the CIA”.

The same US government that today denounces Bin Laden and the Taliban lauded them as “freedom fighters” in the 1980s.

The rulers of the world have no interest in human rights, or in the lives of ordinary people. As Leon Trotsky said over 80 years ago:

“[We have] nothing in common with those bought and paid for moralists who, in response to any terrorist act, make solemn declarations about the ‘absolute value’ of human life. These are the same people who, on other occasions, in the name of other absolute values—for example, the nation’s honour or the monarch’s prestige—are ready to shove millions of people into the hell of war.”

That millions of people around the world passionately hate imperialist US policies is the fault of the US ruling class; of the politicians and businessmen who grow fat through the suffering and death of ordinary people.

The tragedy of the attacks on the US is that ordinary Americans have had to suffer for the genocidal and inhumane policies of their rulers. In answer to the question of where responsibility lies for this senseless loss of life, there can only be one answer: Capitalism.

But whilst we understand the anger directed against America, Marxists are not terrorists.

We utterly oppose the idea that, by killing ordinary people, a tiny minority can change the world for the better. It is only through …

author: Anonymous
title: “There’s this sketchy Dutch black metal band touring Australia …”
content:
I was contacted a little while ago by somebody raising concerns about a couple of upcoming black metal gigs. Below is the text they sent.

There’s this sketchy Dutch black metal band, Helleruin, playing in Melbourne at the Northcote Social Club on September 11 and in Sydney at Crowbar on September 12.

Most of Helleruin’s records have been released on New Era Productions, which has put out a number of releases by fash black metal bands and which is run by Jasper Velzel, a NSBM and RAC musician. In addition, another project of Helleruin’s Carchost — Orewoet — is on the label Heidens Hart, which — along with releasing some far-right stuff — is owned by a former live guitarist of prominent fash band Graveland.

Moreover, a number of the local supporting acts have sketchy connections.

Order of Orias, one of two supports in Melbourne along with Petrol (see below), are on World Terror Committee, which releases fashy stuff and is owned by Sven Zimper, a member of prominent NSBM group Absurd.

Of the bands playing Sydney with Helleruin (Krvna, Pestilential Shadows, Destruktor, Vicissitude, Gravgöt, Grotesque Bliss, Petrol, Blasfemancia and Akhoth) at the ‘Call from the Grave’ festival:

Pestilential Shadows have released music on the Chinese label, GoatowaRex, who are very friendly to NSBM acts. Additionally, PS is part of a collective called Ordo Ater Anguis/Order of the Black Serpent, which includes numerous far right acts. Michael W Ford of Black Funeral appears to be a former Order of Nine Angles (09A) member in the United States who — after distancing himself from O9A — attempted to formulate a social Darwinist version of the Satanic Temple (lol), which coalesce around the Australian fash-friendly label, Dark Adversary. Indeed, one of the members of PS is also a member of Varw, a band on Dark Adversary. Further, Akhoth released a demo, ‘Storm of Pagan Fury’, on CD on Dark Adversary this year.

Grotesque Bliss are on Iron Bonehead which, along with the suspect name, appears to be run by a (if only barely) crypto-fascist.

Destruktor is on a label, Hells Headbangers, which has previously released and re-released stuff by Satanic Warmaster and Deströyer 666, including re-releasing Deströyer 666’s debut album, ‘Unchain the Wolves’, on a few different mediums over the last few years. Additionally, Inquisition had a few releases on Hells Headbangers after their lead singer (who is also a Satanist pedo) released openly fash music on fash label Satanic Skinhead Propaganda (a label which the Iron Bonehead guy sold in his old fash-friendly record store).

The most recent (2024) EP of Krvna, formally of PS, was released on Zazen Sounds, run by Greek nazi black metaller Acherontass of Αχέροντας (Krvna played guest guitar on their most recent album). For what it’s also worth, Third Eye Temple — the Polish label on which Krvna’s 2022 album was released — have released one split and re-issued an EP by Voidhanger, a side project of Polish far right black metallers, Infernal War.

Finally, Petrol were previously on a cancelled bill with Gurn. They also played a gig with Japanese band Abigail, who are signed to Nuclear Now Productions, a fash-friendly label linked to Iron Bonehead (similarly exposed by the nsbmboneheads blog linked above). In addition, Petrol played at Crowbar Sydney last year with Bolzer (see nsbmboneheads blog), who released all but their last record on Iron Bonehead. The other headliner was Portal, who have released lots of records on Hells Headbangers including, recently, a split with Blood of Kingu — a side-project of the Ukrainian ultra-nationalists from Drudkh — on the label in 2014.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Bob Brown: Australian government ‘culpable’ for climate disasters like Nepal
content:
Former Greens leader Bob Brown said Australia is “culpable” for the devastation in Nepal because it was not acting seriously on the dangers of carbon emissions changing the climate.

Australia is co-hosting the COP31 summit in November, along with Türkiye. Yet despite talking up climate action, Labor set about lowering expectations after it was first elected in 2022.

Green Left’s Alex Bainbridge spoke with former Greens leader Bob Brown about Labor’s refusal to take climate action seriously, even though it is a co-host of COP31.

What do you think of Labor’s approach to the climate emergency and does Australia deserve to be co-hosting COP31?

The symbolism of turning on Beetaloo in the wake of the Nepali avalanche disaster is very hard to ignore.

But this Labor government, much like the far-right alternatives, is captured by the corporate sector, including Woodside and BHP, selling off Australian’s rights for a secure future.

They won’t be the only culpable governments in Türkiye, however. Labor appears to be better than Pauline Hanson, but One Nation and Labor are both culpable of making climate change worse.

Federal Labor is set to debate the so-called “improved native forest management” method. Supporters claim it is going save some native forests. However, it allows state governments to earn carbon credits to then plough back into an already dodgy carbon trading system. Should saving forests be contingent on companies being able to buy carbon credits?

We’ve got more than 600 national parks in Australia, and world heritage areas, and they’ve all been set aside for the nation’s future because of their natural and cultural heritage values.

They were never set aside because of the dollars that could be made out of it.

But we’ve got a watershed moment; if Labor gets away with this, we have this new dynamic whereby future national parks will depend, to some degree or another, on whether the corporate sector can extract money as a result.

The NSW Chris Minns Labor government went to the last election in 2023 promising a great koala national park. It never put a condition on that, nor would it have, because polls showed that 80% of Labor voters wanted that park created and want koalas saved.

But, since the election, Minns has added a rider that you cannot have the koala park unless you agree to a scheme that measures the carbon absorbed by the saved forest and sells it to polluters as a cheap “offset”, so they can continue polluting. This way the polluting corporation can keep putting greenhouse gases into the atmosphere and make climate change worse.

We need to look at this through the lens of United Nations Secretary General António Guterres, who has repeatedly said the quickest and cheapest way to deal with climate change is to stop logging forests. This Minns manoeuvre destroys that advantage.

Energy minister Chris Bowen is once again criticising the Greens’ decision in 2009 to block the flawed carbon pollution reduction scheme (CPRS), which we called the “continue polluting regardless scheme”. There’s a lot of rewriting of that history. Looking back, were the Greens right to block the CPRS?

How do you respond to Labor’s argument that the decision set the climate movement back by a decade?

Bowen and Labor have a blind spot on the Julia Gillard years, when the Greens got Labor to put through the carbon pricing scheme in 2011, which was a world leader and really did make a difference because it almost instantly lowered greenhouse gases emissions for the first time in decades and lowered electricity prices.

The CPRS, which came two years before that, was flawed. It had been negotiated by then Prime Minister Kevin Rudd with the Coalition. It was only when the Coalition pulled out that they said, “Well, now the Greens have got to put it through.” The Greens said we’ll amend it and they said “No”.

Large sections of the Canberra press gallery have glossed over the real action that was needed to tackle climate change and which the Greens got two years later with Gillard. Our scheme was so effective that [former Coalition Prime Minister] Tony Abbott had to try to dismantle as much of it as he could.

Let me just go back to the CPRS. The Greens said it is simply feather bedding for multinational polluters and we are not going to pass it. The media said: “The Greens have had it. There’s five Greens in the parliament. They’re going to lose at the next election.”

At the next election, our vote went up by 50% and …

author: Mick Armstrong
title: FROM THE ARCHIVE—US imperialism (November 2002)
content:
Four weeks after the 9/11 attacks, the US invaded Afghanistan. By early 2002, the Bush administration began making the public case for invading Iraq, declaring the country part of an “axis of evil” with Iran and North Korea. Undersecretary of State John Bolton soon expanded the list to include Cuba, Libya and Syria. (The name “axis of resistance”, including Iran, Syria, Hezbollah and Hamas, was reportedly coined in response to all this.)

It became clear very quickly, however, that the analysis laid out in our 12 September editorial was substantially correct. In March 2022, Condoleezza Rice, then Bush’s national security adviser, admitted to the New Yorker’s Nicholas Lemann that, in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, she had asked senior national security staff to think about how to “capitalise on these opportunities”, which were “shifting the tectonic plates in international politics” to US advantage. “I really think this period is analogous to 1945 to 1947”, she said. “And it’s important to try to seize on that and position American interests and institutions and all of that before they harden again.”

It is obvious to more and more people that the [impending] US war on Iraq has got absolutely nothing to do with defending democracy or stopping “terrorism”, let alone with liberating the people of Iraq. It is a good old-fashioned imperialist war—like when the British sent in the gunboats to prove to the locals who was boss.

The September 11 terrorist attacks were a godsend for George Bush. They gave the US establishment carte blanche to accelerate military expenditure, crack down on dissent at home and to adopt a much more aggressive posture on the world stage.

Following hard on the heels of the Afghan war, the war on Iraq is just another step by the US ruling class to assert its military and economic dominance over global capitalism.

But why Iraq?

At one level it doesn’t matter all that much to the US who they attack. They are out to demonstrate that the US is the sole superpower that can assert its might right across the globe, and provided they are victorious, the Pentagon planners don’t care whether the next target is North Korea, Sudan, Colombia, Central Asia or Libya.

The strategists of Bush’s “war on terrorism” have spelt it out very clearly—they are planning permanent war, with the US military engaged in country after country. They want to establish a US armed presence in every corner of the globe and over the next decade they want to launch a first strike nuclear attack somewhere.

The US ruling class increasingly see the enormous military superiority they have over all their capitalist rivals as their key bargaining chip to shore up the profits of US multinationals and to force their economic competitors in Europe, Japan and China to make concessions to them in terms of opening up markets for US goods. Taking out Iraq will be a graphic illustration to all the other powers of the US’s willingness to resort to force to protect its interests.

There are of course additional factors. To start with—oil.

The Middle East has long been of central importance to US imperialism because of its enormous oil reserves—control over which is vital to the interests of all the advanced capitalist powers. By putting an upstart like Saddam Hussein in his place, not only does the US military defend the economic interests of its multinational oil companies, it also gives the US vital leverage over Japan and the European Union, which are more dependent on Middle Eastern oil than the US itself.

Partly it is settling scores with Saddam. The US backed Saddam’s brutal rise to power in Iraq to crush the powerful working-class movement there and to secure Western interests. They armed him to the teeth with chemical and biological weapons.

But then he got too big for his boots, and as with so many other US-backed dictators—Milosevic in Serbia, Noriega in Panama, the Taliban in Afghanistan—they moved to eliminate him.

The problem was that Saddam was more cunning than most; he managed to survive defeat in the Gulf War and has played fast and loose with the US for years. His defiance encourages other lesser powers to stand up to US hegemony.

This makes him a marked man whom Bush is determined to eliminate. Cutting Saddam down sends a message to every other US client state—don’t step out of line or you’re next.

The other reason that Iraq and Afghanistan are important to the US is China. The US establishment sees China as the rising …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Two fossil states, one public bill
content:
Australia digs fossil fuels; Türkiye burns them. One exports coal, the other imports it.

Then came Woodside — a nine-year liquefied natural gas (LNG) deal, signed weeks before COP31 was awarded to Antalya. Two states, one fossil fuel relationship, one climate summit.

The partnership shows how both governments talk about climate finance and what they refuse to name.

Australia is hosting a leaders’ summit in Fiji in October and then Tuvalu. Why Tuvalu? Because the island is sinking and it makes a ready-made stage. But county’s leaders are not coming — Germany, Mexico and South Korea are sending ministers instead. The Pacific Resilience Facility has a target of $500 million; only $172 million has been pledged.

Had COP31 been held in Kaurna Yerta/Adelaide, the bill could have reached $2 billion.

The summits in Dubai and Baku were funded by petrostates — fossil fuel companies paid for access. Now it is Türkiye’s turn.

The answer to who pays is buried in the COP31 hosting agreement, passed by the Turkish Grand National Assembly on July 30. It lists many cost items but attaches no estimated price to any — a blank cheque.

The total is estimated to have already exceeded half a billion dollars — surpassing the cost of the NATO Summit held in Ankara just weeks earlier, and COP31 (Conference of Parties for the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change) has not even begun.

This money will come from the public. But this is not what the “climate finance” conversation is about.

The tourism revenue from the summit will flow to the big hotels. Türkiye’s Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Ersoy, is the co-founder of ETS Tour, one of Türkiye’s largest tour operators and Voyage Hotels.

The agreement passed with barely a question asked. Only one party filed a dissenting note. Five deputies voted against, 22 abstained; 38 opposition deputies voted in favour, while 115 opposition deputies did not turn up to vote at all.

The pattern is familiar; a 2019 law exempting thermal power plants from pollution filters passed in the same near-silence — until we published the attendance records.

Parliament had chosen silence; the public named it and the president was forced to veto the law he had just been handed. What is being named this time is different: the absence of 115 deputies.

Climate change is a capital transfer built on fossil fuels. What we need is an end to the destructive system the public is financing, not more finance to work within it.

Türkiye spent US$727 billion on fossil fuel imports between 2003 and 2022. Even 10% of that figure would constitute a major source of climate finance. But that money is already spent — feeding the fossil fuel system.

Asphalt, concrete, roads, buildings are fossil fuel systems too.

COP31 will be held on land built over farmland for the EXPO 2016 fair — used once then left idle — with a 150,000 square metre asphalt car park added for the occasion. They just are not named as climate policy.

The foundations of Türkiye’s largest climate-changing corporations came together in June to launch the “Philanthropy for Climate” initiative.

Who are the founding signatories? Koç Holding, which operates Türkiye’s largest oil refinery, Sabancı Holding, which owns Enerjisa’s coal and gas plants and Çimsa cement operations is a key player and TAV Airports, which operates Antalya Airport in the city hosting COP31.

They claim to be “taking responsibility for the climate”, but laundering it is a more accurate description.

What makes it worse is that environmental organisations, education and health bodies have signed on.

Sixteen organisations in Türkiye pushed back saying: “Those who are changing the climate cannot clear their own name”.

Other ecology and environment movements had no position. That silence gave Philanthropy for Climate exactly what it needed: civil society legitimacy.

“Climate finance” may be the most content-free phrase in the climate debate. Türkiye received billions of dollars of climate finance from the World Bank, among others, and its emissions kept rising.

The public money going to fossil fuel imports is another form of financing, but it will not appear on the agenda of climate negotiations.

A climate activist flying in from Australia for COP31 will land at TAV’s airport, stay in a hotel built by the minister’s company and sit in rooms where the “finance” being discussed will be none of the above.

This is not a COP problem; it is proof of exactly what COP is …

author: Tom Bramble
title: FROM THE ARCHIVE—War abroad and repression at home (November 2005)
content:
This is an edited version of an article written in response to the 2005 Anti-Terrorism Bill, which was rammed through parliament by Prime Minister John Howard’s Coalition government with the support of the Labor Party the following month (December 2005). 

The legislation gave security agencies the power to detain and question suspects for up to fourteen days without charge; and it made it a crime for people who had been detained to tell anyone about it. It also gave police the power to impose control orders on suspects for up to a year. 

Further, it reintroduced the crimes of “sedition” and “seditious intention”. The latter includes the crimes of intending “to bring the sovereign [the federal government] into hatred or contempt” or to “urge disaffection” against the constitution, the government or the parliament. 

Bramble noted that “the Australian government has passed 26 laws that restrict civil rights in the name of ‘combating terrorism’”. By 2021, the

Australian Financial Review

 could report that “more than 130 pieces of national security legislation” had been enacted since 9/11.

Howard’s latest “anti-terrorism” laws, due to take effect by the end of this year, are a drastic attack on the civil rights of all ordinary Australians and Muslims in particular. These laws are the direct product of September 11, but not in the way that our government would have us believe. 

Wars do not involve just military forces but ideological warfare as well. The enemy has to be demonised—to be rendered sub-human in order to justify its slaughter. In addition, an “enemy within” has to be created to cement “national unity” at home. 

Thousands of Muslim residents of the USA, UK and Australia have been subject to police harassment, detention without trial, secret hearings, censorship and torture. Their homes have been raided, their communications intercepted, and infiltrators and provocateurs planted in their communities. At the same time, the climate of anti-Muslim racism stoked by the “war on terror” has resulted in an increase in harassment on the streets, with Muslims being abused and assaulted.

Since 9/11, the Australian government has passed 26 laws that restrict civil rights in the name of “combating terrorism”. Howard’s new laws represent the further acceleration of state repression. Their purpose is not to keep us safe on public transport but to foster a climate of fear, suspicion and racism, the better to keep us divided. Such an environment helps Howard push through his unpopular agenda at home of union-busting, locking up refugees, privatisation of Telstra and the destruction of Medicare.

Under these new laws, Muslims in particular will be subject to control orders which allow people deemed in secret court hearings to be “terrorist risks” to be electronically tagged. Those subject to control orders will be subject for 12 months to travel bans, restrictions on whom they can meet, and bans on communicating with associates by telephone, internet or email. The government has already announced that it has its eye on 800 Muslim suspects

The legal tradition of

habeas corpus

, whereby people cannot be held unless charged with an offence, will be trashed. Preventative detention allows the police and ASIO to secretly lock up people for up to 48 hours and, with the assistance of state police, up to 14 days. Preventative detention applies not to people who have allegedly committed an offence or even alleged to have any information in relation to an offence, but merely on suspicion of what they may do in future.

It will be a crime for an organisation to “advocate” terrorism, which includes “directly or indirectly counselling or urging” a terrorist act, or “directly praising” terrorism. The range of groups that can be banned as terrorist will be dramatically widened and any of their members, supporters or financial donors can be imprisoned for years.

In order to push all of this through, the AFP and ASIO are undergoing a massive expansion, with ASIO growing from 584 officers in 2001 to 1860 by 2010. With this expansion in numbers goes ever-increasing powers: use of CCTV surveillance, the power to secretly enter and search premises, intercept communication and seize material. The AFP will have new powers to stop, question and search people on the street, seize documents and obtain airline passenger information.

The Vietnam Syndrome

The “war on terror” has a second major purpose: to overcome once and for all the Vietnam …

author: Pip Hinman
title: Nepal disaster a climate warning for COP31
content:
The disaster in Nepal, Tibet and China has been described as being like a “horror movie” — even by those in the midst of the catastrophe.

Just as the wildfires in Europe and the Black Summer bushfires in Australia, it is hard to imagine just how catastrophic these climate-fuelled events can be — until they happen — and even then, it is hard to get one’s head around.

But climate scientists have warned for decades that in an increasingly warming world — the result of human-induced activity — catastrophic events are hard to predict but they will happen.

Scientists have also warned for decades that tipping points — critical limits in the Earthʼs climate and planetary sub-systems (rainforests and ice sheets) where small additional changes can trigger major and potentially irreversible shifts that continue on their own — will be more frequent.

They have also pointed out the injustice associated with these disasters: countries that had the least to do with the problem are the worst affected. This is what we are seeing in Nepal.

The climate emergency — seen today in fires across Europe, the melting glaciers in the Himalayas and the developing El Niño in the Southern Ocean — is not new. But it is getting worse. Just as shocking as the catastrophic events themselves, is that those in power refuse to do anything to avert it.

This is where we need more focus. Once, the Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese told us that the climate emergency was the “greatest moral issue of our time”. Now, asked by reporters if the world has to take some collective responsibility for not doing enough on climate change, he said that “now’s the time … to focus … very much on people who are incredibly traumatised”.

The most useful way Australia could reassure people who are traumatised is by taking a proactive approach to this global problem, to which this country, a major coal and gas exporter, makes a significant contribution.

Albanese and several other ministers in Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum last week were keen to play down climate in favour of “security”, including the Pacific Policing initiative, which involves Australia training new recruits to counter “transnational crime”. But the climate crisis is the most serious transnational crime of them all.

Even Palauan President Surangel Whipps, not renown for being outspoken on climate, said: “It is hard to overstate the depth of emotion for those of us living on the frontline after having fought so hard to put the 1.5 degree limit at the heart of the Paris Agreement … calls for greater ambition are no longer enough — we need to see an urgent and unprecedented increase in political will and investment in a climate safe future.”

A United Nations Environment Program report, released in September, warns that global temperature rise is set to cross 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels by 2030. “There are no good outcomes in remaining above 1.5°C,” it said.

It said “potential tipping points” include irreversible changes to ice sheets, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (the system of ocean currents that acts as a global conveyor belt carrying warm surface water north and cold deep water south) and the erasure of the Amazon rainforest. All these would lead to intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss and submersion of small island states and low-lying coastal cities.

It said warming up to or less than 3°C would mean glaciers could lose more than a quarter of their mass by 2100 and sea levels would rise by 12.5 centimetres. Apart from severe damage to human health, food security, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies, it would mean “crossing thresholds that become difficult or impossible to reverse on human timescales”.

There is debate among climate scientists, some of whom say the UN is underplaying the scale of the global warming disaster. Climate Brink said: “Most forecasts predict that 2027 will set records, with the global average temperature reaching levels we would not expect until the late 2030s”.

The Nepal disaster is a reminder that climate change is the greatest security threat of our time. Burning of fossil fuels, which leads to more trapped greenhouse gases, continues to contribute to the accumulation of energy in the Earth system that, in turn, leads to uninhabitable temperatures.

Australia, a co-host of the COP31 in Türkiye, will argue that it is on track to reach its 2030 target of cutting emissions by 43% below 2005 levels …

author: Liz Walsh
title: FROM THE ARCHIVE—‘End this disgusting war’: an interview with Malalai Joya (November 2010)
content:
Afghanistan was supposed to be “the good war”—the war to catch Osama bin Laden, to liberate the women suffering under the Taliban regime, to bring democracy and rights to the population. It was all lies. The Washington Post reported in October 2001, on the eighth day of the invasion, that the Taliban was offering to turn over bin Laden to a neutral third country to end the US invasion. But the US government rejected the offer. 

Moreover, none of the 9/11 terrorists was Afghan; most were Saudi nationals, including bin Laden. But that country was a key US ally. The elections in Afghanistan, when they came, were a sham. And the country’s women were pawns in a US imperial plan to tear through the Middle East—the Americans moved on to Iraq in no time. 

One of the loudest voices of resistance to both US imperialism and the old and emerging Afghan “order” was Malalai Joya. She sat down with Socialist Alternative’s Liz Walsh in 2010, nine years after the beginning of the invasion and occupation of her country.

For nine long years, the United States and its allies have been tearing apart Afghanistan. And still their occupation grinds on. Few Afghan voices have emerged in condemnation of this barbarous war as forcefully as Malalai Joya’s.

Joya emerged on the international stage as a fierce anti-war figure and fighter for women’s rights when she was elected in 2003 to the 

Loya Jirga

, which was convened to ratify Afghanistan’s constitution. It was here that she used her 

maiden speech

 to launch a blistering attack on the warlords present at the gathering.

Joya was elected to the Afghan parliament in 2005, which she used as a platform to continue her courageous denunciation of all who oppress the Afghan people, from Karzai’s corrupt puppet regime to the Taliban insurgency 

and

 the occupation forces.

In 2007, Joya was permanently expelled from the Afghan parliament. Not surprisingly, there have been no words of protest at this attack on democracy from the occupying powers.

Since her expulsion, Joya has travelled the world to bring the truth of the occupation to Western audiences. She is currently on a speaking tour in Australia, where she has addressed refugee rallies, anti-war vigils and university lecture halls. Willing to speak to whoever will listen, Joya found the time to speak with me about her political activism, views on the occupation and hopes for the future.

Joya was not always a political activist. “At first I was a social activist. I didn’t want to be a politician.” For much of the 1990s, while Afghanistan was ruled by the Taliban, Joya worked with the Organisation for Promoting Afghan Women’s Capabilities (OPAWC) to set up underground schools, teaching literacy to girls and adult women.

She herself was educated in a school run by the 

Revolutionary Association of Women of Afghanistan

 (RAWA), while her family lived in a refugee camp in Pakistan, having been forced into exile by the 1979 Soviet invasion. It was here that Joya developed her staunch commitment to the importance of education for girls and women’s rights.

But in the aftermath of the 2001 invasion—faced with a mounting civilian death toll from the American warplanes that rained cluster bombs and white phosphorus from the sky, and a corrupt government filled with the very people responsible for terrorising and pillaging Afghanistan during the vicious civil war that erupted in the 1990s—Joya decided that she needed to intervene politically:

“When I was a social activist, I talked a lot with the people. I loved with them. I cried with them. I heard a lot about their stories, about the crimes these criminals committed against them. In 2003, I decided I couldn’t tolerate it anymore.”

But then she quips, “In the parliament they couldn’t tolerate me”.

Joya argues without hesitation for the troops to get out of Afghanistan:

“The troops only double our misery. We are crushed between two enemies, the warlords and Taliban on one side. They both continue their fascism. And the occupation forces on the other side. They are bombing and doing massacres. In my province, Farah, in one day they killed 150 civilians through bombs.

“It would be much easier for us to fight one enemy than to have to fight two. The occupation gives more money and more guns to these warlords. They are getting more powerful.”

She points out that the Australian government too has been directly aiding the warlords, with 

recent revelations in the media

 that senior …

title: İSİG Council: At least 226 workers died in August
content:
The Workers’ Health and Work Safety Assembly (İSİG) has released its “Work-Related Deaths Report” for August 2026. Accordingly, at least 226 workers died in Turkey in the month of August as a result of workplace accidents and work-related deaths.

The report stated that those who lost their lives included 15 women, 15 children and 16 refugee workers.

According to İSİG data, traffic accidents were the leading cause of worker deaths. In August, 22 percent of worker deaths were caused by traffic accidents.

Traffic accidents were followed by falls from height at 21 percent and deaths caused by crushing and structural collapses at 19 percent.

author: labor4pal
title: Resolution of Labor Movement Support for the Minnesota 15
content:
Whereas, during the winter of 2025-2026 working class people across the United States and across the world watched the people of Minnesota bravely protect their neighbors through resistance to a brutal occupation of federal immigration agents;

Whereas, in the early morning of June 16th, 2026 the federal government arrested activists and community members from the Twin Cities. They arrested union members, teachers, healthcare workers, carpenters and electricians. They arrested organizers of the mass strike on January 23rd and community members who put themselves on the line to defend their neighbors and take a stand against ICE terror.

Whereas, 15 activists have been charged with “conspiracy to impede federal officers,” and are described as “members of Antifa groups” by the federal government. The charges include making anti-ICE statements online, planning and attending anti-ICE protests, and engaging in rapid response and mutual aid to defend our immigrant neighbors.

Whereas, if these charges are upheld, they could criminalize every person who participates in collective action such as rapid response, immigrant defense, mutual aid, and school patrols, in Minnesota and beyond. The implications of such will extend far beyond these defendants and criminalize efforts to resist an increasingly authoritarian federal government;

Whereas, the federal government’s portrayal of the defendants stands in stark contrast to the reality that Minnesotans experienced during months of federal occupation: that throughout that period, residents were subjected to repeated acts of violence, intimidation, and repression.

Whereas, these charges are part of a broader pattern of the Trump administration to punish Minnesota for our fierce and ongoing resistance. It follows similar raids targeting anti-fascist, Black voting rights, and pro-Palestine activists in Georgia, Texas, Michigan, Oregon, and Ohio.

Therefore be it resolved, we, the members of the labor movement listed below stand in unwavering solidarity with the Minnesota 15 defendants, and all those that face state repression for practicing their right to resist and protest;

Be it further resolved that we demand the following:

Return the Abducted & Deported – Reunite the Families!

Drop the Charges Against All Anti-ICE Protesters!

Justice for Renee, Victor, Alex, Keith, Lorenzo, Joan, and All Victims of ICE Violence.

AFSCME Local 529 – Mid-Minnesota Legal Aid Workers Union

Virginia Caucus of Rank and file Educators

Greater Chicago Industrial Workers of the World

Labor for Palestine National Network

Caucus of Rank-and-file Electrical Workers

National Association of Letter Carriers Branch 9

See also: Independent statements of solidarity with the Minnesota 15.

author: Jenny Brown
title: ‘Don’t Privatize Airport Security’ Say Screeners and Flight Attendants on 9/11 Anniversary
content:
Union flight attendants are mourning lost co-workers on the 25-year anniversary of the September 11 attacks. In Chicago today, they’re joining with Transportation Security Officers to defend airport security gains made in the last quarter-century.


“I was there. I lost my friends,” said Sara Nelson, president of the Association of Flight Attendants. “Our union made a sacred promise to ensure that such a tragedy is never repeated.” She described the Trump administration’s attempts to privatize airport security as a danger to the public as well as the 55,000 members of her union.


At the time of the September 11 attacks, airport security relied on a patchwork of private contractors, “driven by corporate bottom lines and cost-cutting,” Nelson

wrote

 in a July letter to Congress.


“We don’t have to theorize about what that may look like because we have been through this before and witnessed the devastating and deadly consequences,” said Government Employees (AFGE) President Everett Kelley on July 21, after a new privatization scheme, TSA Gold+, was revealed.


With the creation of TSA in 2001, all workers became direct employees of the federal government, with uniform standards across airports. The workers unionized in 2011, becoming members of AFGE Council 100, which now represents 47,000.


ATTACKING THE UNION


Since coming into office in 2025, the Trump administration has been trying to get rid of the union at TSA, and privatize airport security. Union members say the administration is following the plans laid out in the right-wing Project 2025’s

Mandate for Leadership

.


Darrell English, president of AFGE Local 777, said rich contracts are being dangled for tech companies to come in and replace workers. Local 777 represents 2,500 Transportation Security Officers at 19 airports in Illinois and Wisconsin.


“They’re giving these contracts to these billionaires for their technology,” said English, a lead officer with 21 years at the agency. “And that technology is going to reduce the staffing levels at airports for TSA officers.


“It's all about gaining that money, the financial contracts, through TSA,” he said.


Kelley called the privatization plans a “major departure and step backwards from the aviation screening security system that Congress created in the wake of the Sept. 11th terrorist attacks.”


Nelson wrote to Congress urging rejection of David Cummins, a nominee for TSA director who is committed to privatization and opposes collective bargaining at TSA. Cummins was confirmed by the Senate 51-47 on August 7.


PARTIAL WIN


The unions notched a partial win when Cummins

backed down

 from “TSA Gold+,” much touted by the Trump administration and his predecessor, Ha Nguyen McNeill.


AFGE leaders said they only learned about the TSA Gold+ program from the press in July, even though it had been in development for many months. When the government didn’t respond to a request for relevant documents, AFGE sued for their release.


The program would have allowed airports to completely privatize their security operations, including bringing in their own equipment. “TSA Gold+ would have put private contractors in control not only of security screening functions but the screening technology itself,” said Nelson.


But airport managers were skeptical.  Only three airports seemed to be on track to implement it, in Tampa, Des Moines, and Charleston, South Carolina. Then the largest, Tampa International Airport, announced August 24 that after a months-long evaluation, it would be sticking with the existing TSA workforce.


That same day, Cummins announced the end of TSA Gold+, but privatization plans would go forward under a new scheme: Horizon 25 Strategy. It includes expanding the small, already existing Screening Partnership Program (SPP), where screeners work for a private company. The largest airport to use it is San Francisco.


The Trump administration’s proposed 2027 budget would cut thousands of TSO jobs. According to the union, the budget would eliminate 14 percent of the workforce, or 8,400 positions. The administration’s plan, the


union said in July

, is that private contractors would replace 4,500 screening workers “through a proposed mandatory expansion of the Screening Partnership Program to include all small and non-hub airports.”


Only 20 of the country’s 440 commercial airports now use private screening under the SPP, which was rolled out in 2004.  But that would expand to 220 under the …

73 ji van karkeran di sektora avahisaziyê de, 58 di çandiniyê de, 45 di pîşesaziyê de û 41 jî di sektora xizmetguzariyê de dixebitîn. Tenê 7 ji wan endamên sendîkayekê bûn. 


Meclîsa İSİGê, ji sedî 68ê daneyan ji çapemeniya neteweyî, ji sedî 32yê wan jî ji hevalên kar û malbatên karkaran, pisporên ewlehiya karî, bijîşkên cihê karî, sendîka û çapemeniya herêmî berhev kiriye.


Di meha Tebaxê de karker herî zêde di beşên avahîsazî, guhestin, metal û çandiniyê de mirin e.

Karkerên koçber di bin çerxa bêewlehiyê de ne, di bin şert û mercên herî xirab de tên xebitandin. 


38 karker temenê wan di navbera 18-29an de bûn, 80 karker temenê wan di navbera 30-49an de bûn, 63 karker di navbera 50-64an de û 21 karker jî temenê wan 65 û berjortir bû. Temenê 9 karkeran nehat zanîn.


Li gorî rapora di Tebaxê de 15 jin û 16 karkerên koçber jiyana xwe ji dest dan.

title: PERTUIS : non au permis de tuer ! - évènement statique le 20 septembre
content:
Le Collectif Antifasciste Sud Lubéron et Gabi L'antilope Queer du Lubéron s'associent pour organiser un moment de convivialité et de radicalité en ruralité.


Le 20 Sept à partir de 12 h - Cours de la République - Une grande gratuiterie Antifa - Des prises de paroles sont au menu de cette belle journée.


Pourquoi se réunir le 20 septembre ? Une réponse à l'appel du SAVE


En ce dimanche 20 septembre, nous nous réunissons pour répondre à l'appel lancé par SAVE (Stop Aux Violences d'État), et qui s'oppose à l'adoption de la proposition de loi 691. Cette loi, qui encadre la « présomption de légitime défense » pour les forces de l'ordre, octroie aux policiers la possibilité de faire usage de leur arme à feu dans l'exercice de leurs fonctions sans être inquiétés par la justice.


Les violences policières sont déjà aussi fréquentes qu'impunies ; en France, environ 6 % à 10 % des agents de police mis en cause pour des violences volontaires font l'objet d'une condamnation par la justice. Sur ces mises en causes, seulement 8 % font l'objet d'une condamnation (Politis, 2022).


En 2021, 83% des peines d'emprisonnement prononcées pour violences volontaires par les « PDAP » (personnes dépositaires de l'autorité publique) étaient assorties d'un sursis (contre 55% dans la population générale). Nous ne croyons pas à la prison. Mais il semblerait que celleux qui les administrent et les remplissent n'y croient pas non plus lorsque vient le temps de juger les agents de l'État autoritaire en uniforme au lieu d'emprisonner nos camarades.


Le projet de loi 691 n'est pas un changement brusque de stratégie de la part des gouvernants, ni une menace nouvelle ; il s'inscrit dans un continuum, représente une étape dans la longue escalade des violences policières et de leur légitimation par l'État. Les fatalistes nous demanderont donc peut-être pourquoi tirer la sonnette d'alarme maintenant. Nous leur répondons que si la situation est déjà sinistre, nous pouvons être sûr·es qu'elle ne fera qu'empirer au fil de la séquence potentiellement fasciste, et dans tous les cas répressive, qui se profile à l'horizon.


La pétition déposée par SAVE à l'assemblée nationale a reçu 732 086 signatures, un nombre qui dépasse de plus de sept fois le seuil réglementaire de 100 000 signatures. Pourtant, aucun débat en séance publique n'a été organisé pour répondre à cette large mobilisation populaire. Alors il est plus que jamais nécessaire de se réunir dans la rue - pour faire entendre notre colère, rappeler notre puissance collective, et nous opposer aux décisions prises sans nous, pendant qu'il est encore possible de le faire sans que les forces de l'ordre puissent impunément prendre les vies des citoyens récalcitrants, jugés


nuisibles ou gênants pour le déploiement d'une politique d'étranglement répressif.


_ Pourquoi une gratuiterie ? Remplacer la violence gratuite par la gratuité de la vie


Nous aurions tort de penser qu'hors des grands centres urbains paupérisés, la question des violences policières ne nous concerne pas ; ici comme ailleurs, à une échelle différente, les caméras de surveillance se multiplient, les mairies durcissent leurs lignes. Les policiers agressent les populations marginalisées, qui sont peu être moins nombreuses, mais aussi plus repérables et donc plus facilement ciblées pour cette même raison. Les premières personnes visées par cette loi et par l'attention appuyée de la police sont aussi présent.es dans nos campagnes, qu'il s'agisse des voyageur·ses, des descendant·esde l'immigration post-coloniale ou des travailleur·ses migrant.es. Pour autant, être concerné·es au même titre que les villes nesignifie pas forcément se mobiliser de la même manière. Ici, la distance géographique entre les lieux de vie et leurs topographies respectives font perdre son sens au rituel de la manifestation combative de masse.


Le discours dominant veut à tout prix nous faire croire que nos campagnes sont des lieux atomisés, d'isolation, des lieux où le racisme, la xénophobie et la méfiance sont des valeurs à défendre au nom du respect des traditions ou des territoires. C'est à nous qu'il incombe de leur donner tort et de bouder leur (di)vision du monde. C'est pourquoi nous vous invitons à occuper et animer avec nous l'espace public en participant à une gratuiterie. Vêtements, matériel scolaire, jouets pour enfants, vaisselle inutilisée : tout item utile est le bienvenu, à condition qu'il ne soit pas vendu mais donné ! Un vide grenier sans argent …
